To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
alterations in the gut microbiota trajectory in the first months of life may predispose to CD.

infants at familial risk for developing celiac disease (n=10) had a distinct trajectory of gut microbiome and immune markers in the first 6 months of life compared to healthy controls (n=10), suggesting that alterations in the microbiome may predispose to celiac disease.

the gut microbiota of infants with CD showed alterations in diversity and in the relative abundance of several bacterial species, including Bifidobacteria, which may influence the immune maturing process and predispose them to CD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new hypothesis that the development of celiac autoimmunity may be associated with a dysbiotic microbiota and an impaired immune system.
the development of a mathematical model for the analysis of the gut microbiota in early infancy, which may predict the development of celiac.
the study of the intestinal microbiota and the immune response of the intestine in infants who develop celiac disease (celiac disease) and in healthy infants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the microbiota of infants at risk of developing CD is altered and may influence the development of immune responses, but further studies are warranted to determine whether the microbiota alterations observed are causal or consequential to CD.
alterations in gut microbiota and immune maturation may precede the onset of CD in genetically predisposed infants.
alterations in the developing gut microbiota in infancy may be associated with an increased risk of CD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the gut microbial profile of infants with celiac disease is altered and that these changes may be associated with the development of CD.
a healthy gut microbiota is associated with a higher diversity of the microbiota, and a lower diversity of the microbiome is associated with CD development.

the microbiome is not just a passive bystander but is actively involved in the development of the immune system and that the gut microbiota can be a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of celiac disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the gut microbiota of infants at CD risk is characterized by a lower diversity at 6 months compared to that of healthy children.
alterations in the gut microbiota in the first months of life may predict CD development.

the microbiota of infants at CD risk who developed the disease was characterized by a reduced diversity, with a lower proportion of Bifidocateriae spp. and higher Enterococcaceae and Enterobacteriaceae, compared to infants at CD risk that remained healthy.
